mentions.quote: he must not provoke Brahmanas; for they, being angered, could slay him immediately, with his army and vehicles.
mentions.role: subject — sacred class whose wrath is fatal to kings

mentions.quote: By whom fire was made to consume all things, and the great ocean undrinkable, and the waning Soma made to wax again
mentions.role: agent of cosmic feats ascribed to angered Brahmanas

mentions.quote: They who, being angered, could create other worlds and other world-protectors, and could make gods into non-gods
mentions.role: subject — limitless creative and destructive power

mentions.quote: They on whom the worlds and the gods always depend for support, and whose wealth is the Veda itself
A Brahmana, whether unlearned or learned, is a great deity
even if they engage in all kinds of undesirable actions, Brahmanas are to be honored in every way; for that is the supreme deity.
service alone to the Brahmanas who know the Veda, who are householders and are famous, is the highest Dharma for a Shudra

entities.description: The priestly varna, depicted as semi-divine beings whose anger can destroy kings and remake worlds, and to whom all other varnas owe service.
entities.justification: The window's central argument is the inviolable supremacy of the Brahmana class, grounded across multiple verses (313–319, 334) in both cosmological and practical terms.

mentions.quote: When the Kshatra power has grown too great against the Brahmanas in every way, the Brahma power itself shall be the restrainer; for the Kshatra is born from the Brahma.
mentions.role: subject — warrior power checked by priestly power

mentions.quote: From water, fire arose; from the Brahma, the Kshatra; from stone, iron.
The Kshatra does not prosper without the Brahma; the Brahma does not increase without the Kshatra.

entities.description: The warrior-ruler power, said to be born from the Brahma and to require its guidance, unable to prosper independently.
entities.justification: Three consecutive verses (320–322) work out the cosmological and political relationship between Brahma and Kshatra as interdependent yet hierarchically ordered.

mentions.quote: For Prajapati, having created cattle, entrusted them to the Vaishya; and to the Brahmana and the king, he entrusted all the subjects.
mentions.role: divine creator who assigns cosmic duties to each varna

entities.description: The Lord of Creatures who, in the text's cosmogony, created cattle and assigned them to the Vaishya while entrusting all human subjects to Brahmanas and kings.
entities.justification: Prajapati is invoked as the originary authority for the economic and social division of labor among the varnas (Mn_9.327).

mentions.quote: the waning Soma made to wax again
mentions.role: cosmic beneficiary of Brahmana ritual power

entities.description: The lunar deity and sacred drink whose waxing was restored by the power of Brahmanas, cited as evidence of their cosmic efficacy.
entities.justification: Soma's renewal is listed alongside taming fire and the ocean as one of three legendary cosmic acts performed by Brahmanas (Mn_9.314).

mentions.quote: By whom fire was made to consume all things
just as fire, whether consecrated or unconsecrated, is a great deity
Even in cremation grounds, the brilliant fire is not defiled; and when oblations are offered to it in sacrifices, it increases yet more.
From water, fire arose; from the Brahma, the Kshatra; from stone, iron.
mentions.role: element in a cosmogonic series of elemental derivations

entities.description: Fire as both elemental force and deity, used as the primary analogy for the Brahmana's inherent sacredness regardless of moral state.
entities.justification: The fire analogy is developed across three consecutive verses (317–318, 321) to ground Brahmana supremacy in the nature of sacred fire.

mentions.quote: a Vaishya, having received the consecrating rites and having taken a wife, should be ever engaged in economics and in the protection of cattle.
For Prajapati, having created cattle, entrusted them to the Vaishya
a Vaishya should not have the desire, 'I will not protect the cattle'
one should know this rule of action, in order, for the Vaishya and the Shudra.

entities.description: The merchant-farmer varna divinely tasked by Prajapati with protection of cattle and mastery of trade, agriculture, and commercial knowledge.
entities.justification: Verses 326–333 constitute an extended specification of Vaishya duties, including cattle-keeping, commerce, weights, languages, and seed-knowledge.

mentions.quote: service alone to the Brahmanas who know the Veda, who are householders and are famous, is the highest Dharma for a Shudra, leading to the supreme good.
mentions.role: subject whose highest duty is defined as Brahmana service

mentions.quote: Pure, serving the superior, gentle in speech, without arrogance, always taking refuge in the Brahmanas and others, he attains a superior birth.
mentions.role: subject of virtuous conduct leading to better rebirth

entities.description: The fourth varna whose prescribed highest Dharma in this window is service to Vedic Brahmana householders, with the promise of a superior rebirth as reward.
entities.justification: Verses 334–335 close the varna-duty sequence by defining Shudra svadharma as pure service and devotion to higher varnas.

mentions.quote: a king should restrain thieves in his own kingdom and in that of another.
Even when he has reached the greatest distress, he must not provoke Brahmanas
having given to Brahmanas the wealth arising from all fines, having entrusted the kingdom to his son, he should make his last journey in battle.
A king, thus acting, always engaged in the Dharmas of kings, should employ all his servants in what is beneficial for the world.
to the Brahmana and the king, he entrusted all the subjects.
mentions.role: co-guardian of all subjects alongside Brahmanas

entities.description: The royal figure whose duties include suppressing crime, deferring to Brahmanas, distributing fines as gifts to Brahmanas, and finally dying in battle.
entities.justification: The window opens (312) and closes the king's section (323–325) with prescriptions for royal conduct, bracketing the Brahmana-supremacy argument.

mentions.quote: For Prajapati, having created cattle, entrusted them to the Vaishya
mentions.role: divinely assigned charge of the Vaishya

mentions.quote: a Vaishya should not have the desire, 'I will not protect the cattle'; for if a Vaishya wishes it so, they must not be protected by another in any way.

entities.description: Cattle created by Prajapati and exclusively entrusted to the Vaishya varna for protection; no other varna may substitute.
entities.justification: Two consecutive verses (327–328) establish cattle as the defining economic responsibility of the Vaishya, grounded in divine ordinance.

mentions.quote: he must not provoke Brahmanas; for they, being angered, could slay him immediately
A Brahmana, whether unlearned or learned, is a great deity
even if they engage in all kinds of undesirable actions, Brahmanas are to be honored in every way

themes.justification: Verses 313–319 form the window's theological core: Brahmana sacredness is absolute, unconditional, and cosmologically grounded, independent of individual Brahmana conduct.

themes.topic: Complementarity and hierarchy of Brahma and Kshatra powers

mentions.quote: the Kshatra power has grown too great against the Brahmanas… the Brahma power itself shall be the restrainer; for the Kshatra is born from the Brahma.
The Kshatra does not prosper without the Brahma; the Brahma does not increase without the Kshatra.

themes.justification: Verses 320–322 articulate a political theology in which priestly and warrior powers are mutually necessary yet hierarchically ordered, with Brahma as originary.

mentions.quote: This entire eternal rule of action has been declared for a king; one should know this rule of action, in order, for the Vaishya and the Shudra.
a Vaishya, having received the consecrating rites and having taken a wife, should be ever engaged in economics and in the protection of cattle.
service alone to the Brahmanas who know the Veda… is the highest Dharma for a Shudra, leading to the supreme good.

themes.justification: The window concludes with a systematic enumeration of duties for the lower three varnas (king/Kshatriya 323–325, Vaishya 326–333, Shudra 334–335), affirming that each varna has a distinct prescribed path.

mentions.quote: Pure, serving the superior, gentle in speech, without arrogance, always taking refuge in the Brahmanas and others, he attains a superior birth.

themes.justification: The Shudra's virtuous adherence to svadharma is rewarded with a superior rebirth, invoking the karmic framework that underwrites the entire Manusmrti ethics.

themes.topic: Fire as analogy for inherent sacred purity

mentions.quote: just as fire, whether consecrated or unconsecrated, is a great deity
Even in cremation grounds, the brilliant fire is not defiled; and when oblations are offered to it in sacrifices, it increases yet more.

themes.justification: The fire analogy across 317–318 is a deliberate rhetorical device: fire's purity in impure places (cremation grounds) models Brahmana purity despite contact with sin.

mentions.quote: a king should restrain thieves in his own kingdom and in that of another.

themes.justification: Verse 312 closes the preceding anti-theft passage by summarizing the king's obligation to suppress crime as continuous, unwearied duty spanning even foreign territories.

themes.topic: Commercial and agricultural knowledge as Vaishya virtue

mentions.quote: Of jewels, pearls, and coral, of metals and of woven cloth, of perfumes and of savory liquids, he should know the relative value.
He should know the sowing of seeds and the faults and qualities of fields; he should know the application of measures and the application of weights
the excellence and worthlessness of goods, and the advantages and disadvantages of countries, and the profit and loss of merchandise, and the rearing of cattle.

themes.justification: Verses 329–332 provide an unusually concrete catalogue of the commercial and agricultural expertise expected of the Vaishya, reflecting the text's concern for practical varna competence.

themes.topic: Cosmogonic derivation as legitimation of social order

mentions.quote: From water, fire arose; from the Brahma, the Kshatra; from stone, iron. Their all-pervading energy is pacified in their own sources.

themes.justification: The elemental cosmogony (water→fire, Brahma→Kshatra, stone→iron) implicitly legitimates social hierarchy by mapping it onto natural origination sequences, presenting varna order as cosmically given.
